meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Franklin, not Einstein. It is an anonymous early-1980s 12-step recovery saying, first documented in 1981. Here is the evidence.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Franklin — an anonymous 12-step recovery saying
answer.authorDates: Early 1980s · Al-Anon / A.A. / Narcotics Anonymous recovery communities
answer.sourceLine: Benjamin Franklin (d. 1790) never wrote or said this — there is no source in his works, and the Franklin credit only appears online from around 2004. Per Quote Investigator, the saying emerged in early-1980s twelve-step recovery meetings: it was recorded at an Al-Anon meeting in October 1981 and, in a close variant, in a November 1981 Narcotics Anonymous pamphlet (“Insanity is repeating the same mistakes and expecting different results”), then spread through a 1983 novel. It is far more often pinned on Einstein, who also never said it.

source.excerpt: Insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results.
trail: 1981 — recovery rooms. Quote Investigator dates the earliest instances to an Al-Anon meeting (Oct 1981) and a Narcotics Anonymous pamphlet (Nov 1981), not to any famous author.
Not Einstein. Princeton's The Ultimate Quotable Einstein files the line under “Misattributed to Einstein,” and Mental Floss confirms there is no evidence he said it.
Not Franklin. The Wikiquote talk page documents the Franklin credit as a late, sourceless accretion — the earliest Franklin attributions appear around 2004, with no citation in his writings.
source.excerptNote: The wording circulated in twelve-step recovery rooms in the early 1980s; the 1981 Narcotics Anonymous variant read “Insanity is repeating the same mistakes and expecting different results.” The polished “definition of insanity” framing and the Franklin/Einstein bylines were added later.

author.name: Anonymous (12-step recovery fellowships)
author.heading: Where it actually comes from
author.metaLine: Early 1980s · Al-Anon, A.A. & Narcotics Anonymous recovery communities
author.bio: The saying grew out of the shared, deliberately anonymous folk wisdom of twelve-step recovery groups such as Al-Anon, Alcoholics Anonymous, and Narcotics Anonymous, where “insanity” described the self-defeating cycle of repeating harmful behavior. Because these fellowships prize anonymity, no single author was ever recorded — which is precisely why the polished line was later hung on convenient famous names like Einstein and Franklin.

misattribution.heading: A magnet for famous bylines
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-misattributed sayings on the internet. The same anonymous line gets pinned on whichever “smart” name a poster trusts most.

items.why: Nothing in Franklin's published works, letters, or Poor Richard's Almanack contains this line. Per the Wikiquote talk record, Franklin attributions only surface online around 2004 — more than two centuries after his death.

The most common false credit. Princeton's The Ultimate Quotable Einstein lists it under “Misattributed to Einstein,” and Quote Investigator found no evidence he ever said or wrote it — the Einstein byline appears only from around 1990.
Another borrowed-authority credit with no citation in Twain's works; noted alongside the Franklin and Einstein misattributions in the provenance discussions.

Her 1983 novel Sudden Death gives the line to a fictional character, Jane Fulton — an early print appearance, but it postdates the 1981 recovery-meeting attestations and repeats an already-circulating saying rather than coining it.

misattribution.truthLine: The best evidence, per Quote Investigator, is that this is an anonymous twelve-step recovery saying first recorded in 1981 — the famous names came later.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The line is deployed constantly — in boardrooms, therapy, and politics — as if it carried the authority of a scientific genius or a Founding Father. In truth it is anonymous folk wisdom from addiction-recovery meetings, where “insanity” had a concrete, lived meaning: the compulsive repetition of self-destructive behavior.

Stripped of its false bylines, the saying is arguably more honest, not less — it was earned in rooms full of people trying to break exactly the cycle it describes. It is also, strictly, not a real clinical definition of insanity, which is a further reason to be wary of citing it as expert authority.
context.pull: An anonymous line from recovery rooms — not a genius, not a Founding Father.
